reference.source: Occupational and Environmental Respiratory Medicine reference texts
clinicalPearls: Occurs in the flocking industry, where finely cut synthetic fibres (typically nylon, but also polyethylene or rayon) are applied to adhesive-coated backing to create velvet-like surfaces
Respirable fibre fragments generated by cutting and processing are thought to drive the disease rather than the longer intact flock fibres
Presents with cough, breathlessness, and constitutional symptoms, sometimes improving away from work and recurring on return
Characteristic histology is a lymphocytic bronchiolitis and peribronchiolar interstitial inflammation, often described as a distinctive nodular lymphoid pattern
Bronchiolitis obliterans (constrictive bronchiolitis) with airflow obstruction is a recognised and serious manifestation
Clusters of cases in a single workplace are a strong diagnostic clue and should prompt industrial hygiene review
Diagnosis rests on occupational history, imaging, and lung biopsy, since there is no specific confirmatory test
reference.pathophysiology: Machining and cutting of synthetic flock produce ultrafine respirable fibre fragments that deposit in the small airways and distal lung. These particles provoke an immune-mediated inflammatory response centred on the bronchioles, producing lymphocytic bronchiolitis, peribronchiolar lymphoid aggregates, and interstitial infiltration. In some workers the injury evolves to constrictive bronchiolitis with fixed airflow obstruction, while others develop a more diffuse interstitial or organising pneumonia pattern. The disease reflects a reaction to the inhaled polymer fragments rather than fibrogenic mineral dust, and it may improve with removal from exposure.
additionalDifferentials: Respiratory bronchiolitis and other small-airway diseases
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution CT with expiratory imaging to detect mosaic attenuation and air trapping
Detailed occupational history and inquiry into workplace case clusters
Pulmonary function tests including bronchodilator response and lung volumes
Lung biopsy demonstrating lymphocytic bronchiolitis or bronchiolitis obliterans
Bronchoalveolar lavage to characterise inflammatory cells and exclude infection
redFlags: Progressive fixed airflow obstruction indicating established bronchiolitis obliterans
Continued exposure despite symptoms or identified workplace cluster
Rapid functional decline or respiratory failure
Failure to improve after removal from exposure, prompting reassessment
reference.prognosis: Many patients stabilise or improve after leaving exposure, but established bronchiolitis obliterans causes irreversible airflow obstruction, and some progress to significant chronic respiratory impairment despite treatment.
pitfalls: Not recognising the occupational cause and mislabelling it as idiopathic interstitial disease
Overlooking a workplace cluster that would clarify the diagnosis
Relying on inspiratory imaging alone and missing air trapping of small-airway disease
Assuming reversibility when constrictive bronchiolitis is already established
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
management: Removal from further flock and respirable fibre exposure, the key intervention that may allow stabilisation or improvement
Corticosteroids for the lymphocytic bronchiolitis and any interstitial or organising pneumonia component
Inhaled bronchodilators for fixed airflow obstruction in constrictive bronchiolitis
Workplace industrial-hygiene review, dust control and investigation of case clusters to protect co-workers
Serial pulmonary function testing including diffusing capacity to monitor progression
Occupational medicine referral, with lung transplantation considered for progressive, irreversible bronchiolitis obliterans
